claims.claim: Hints of an 'existential attitude' go back to the Stoics, Augustine, Montaigne and Pascal.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [1. Nihilism...]: 'early glimpses of ... the "existential attitude"' in Stoic, Augustine, Montaigne, Pascal

claims.claim: The ideas became a movement only in the nineteenth century.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [1. Nihilism...]: 'not until the nineteenth century ... coalesce into a bona fide intellectual movement'

claims.claim: This happened as a secular, scientific world view replaced the religious frame that gave life direction.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [1. Nihilism...]: 'secular and scientific worldview ... traditional religious framework ... beginning to collapse'

claims.claim: Industry and bureaucracy made society feel impersonal.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [1. Nihilism...]: 'mechanized working conditions and bureaucratic ... increasingly impersonal and alienating social order'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard attacked Hegel's grand system for leaving out the single existing person.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [2.1 Subjective Truth]: Hegel's system 'covers over ... concerns of the existing individual'

claims.claim: Nietzsche diagnosed the coming nihilism.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [1. Nihilism...]: Nietzsche 'most influential and prophetic in diagnosing and conceptualizing the crisis'

claims.claim: Dostoevsky's 'underground man' rebels against being reduced to 'a piano key'.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [4.1 The Anxiety of Choice]: underground man rebels; view 'reduces the human being to ... "a piano key"'

claims.claim: In the twentieth century German thinkers such as Husserl, Jaspers and Heidegger laid more groundwork.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: groundwork laid by 'twentieth-century German philosophers like Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Karl Jaspers'

claims.claim: Phenomenology, the careful description of everyday experience, gave the movement its roots.
claims.evidence: openstax [Existentialism]: 'Existentialism's phenomenological roots'; sep-existentialism [2.3]: 'describe how things are given ... in our average everyday lives'

claims.claim: Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) shaped Sartre and Beauvoir.
claims.evidence: sep-heidegger.txt [intro]: 'Being and Time (1927) ... profoundly influenced ... Sartre's existentialism, Simone de Beauvoir's feminism'

claims.claim: The movement exploded in mid-century France against the backdrop of WWII, the death camps and the atomic bomb.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France ... Second World War, the Nazi death camps'

claims.claim: Sartre's Being and Nothingness appeared in 1943.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [intro]: 'his difficult treatise, Being and Nothingness (1943)'

claims.claim: Gabriel Marcel coined the word 'existentialism' in 1943.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'The word, first introduced by Marcel in 1943'

claims.claim: Who counts as an existentialist is disputed.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'catch-all term ... a case to be made that the term ... does more harm than good'

claims.claim: The term names no single doctrine.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'not a reference to a coherent system ... no unifying doctrine'

claims.claim: Most thinkers grouped under it never used it or rejected it.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'most ... either never used, or actively disavowed, the term'

claims.claim: Only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'only Sartre and Beauvoir explicitly self-identified as "existentialists"'
claims.note: IEP intro also quotes Sartre: 'Existentialism? I don't know what that is.' Not a contradiction, but a curious learner may notice.

claims.claim: Heidegger repudiated Sartre's existentialism in his 'Letter on Humanism' (1947).
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [c. Heidegger]: 'Letter on Humanism' published 1947; 'repudiates any possible connection ... with the existentialism of Sartre'

claims.claim: Both encyclopedias still count Heidegger among its key figures.
claims.evidence: iep [c. Heidegger]: 'Heidegger can be classified as an existentialist thinker'; sep-existentialism [intro]: Heidegger among groundwork 'pioneers'
claims.note: SEP's cited intro frames him as a groundwork pioneer rather than a member; 'key figures' is a fair paraphrase.

claims.claim: Camus gave a 1945 interview titled, in English, 'No, I am not an existentialist'.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [f. Camus]: '"Non, je ne suis pas existentialist" is the title of a famous interview ... 1945'

claims.claim: The SEP places The Myth of Sisyphus squarely in the existentialist tradition.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [1. The Paradoxes...]: 'This essay belongs squarely in the philosophical tradition of existentialism'

claims.claim: Fear and Trembling is by Soren Kierkegaard.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [5.2]: 'In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard draws on ... Abraham'

claims.claim: It was published in 1843.
claims.evidence: sep-kierkegaard.txt [1. Life and Works]: 'Fear and Trembling (1843)'

claims.claim: It uses Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac to ask what faith demands beyond ethics.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [5.2]: God demands he 'kill Isaac'; 'personal truth that is higher than the universal'
claims.note: The source frames it as Abraham's willingness/decision; it never says the sacrifice was not carried out. 'Near-' is the standard description and harmless.

claims.claim: The Gay Science is by Friedrich Nietzsche.
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche.txt [1. Life and Works]: 'The Gay Science (1882, second expanded edition 1887)'

claims.claim: It was published in 1882.
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche.txt [1. Life and Works]: 'The Gay Science (1882 ...)'
claims.note: Learner flag: SEP existentialism 5.3 cites the eternal-recurrence passage as '1887 [1974], §341' (the expanded edition). A learner may see 1882 vs 1887 without explanation.

claims.claim: It poses the eternal-recurrence test: could you will your life again, forever?
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [5.3]: 'In The Gay Science ... "doctrine of eternal recurrence" ... live the same life ... for eternity'

claims.claim: Being and Time is by Martin Heidegger, 1927.
claims.evidence: sep-heidegger.txt [intro]: 'His magnum opus, Being and Time (1927)'

claims.claim: It treats human existence as being-in-the-world.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [2.3]: 'In Being and Time, Heidegger ... existence or "being-in-the-world"'

claims.claim: Human existence is lost in 'the They' until anxiety calls it back.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [5.4]: anxiety 'momentarily "snatches one back" from the tranquilizing routines of "the They"'

claims.claim: The Myth of Sisyphus is by Albert Camus.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [intro]: Camus's question 'which launches The Myth of Sisyphus'

claims.claim: It was published in 1942.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [3. Suicide...]: 'released The Stranger in June 1942 and The Myth of Sisyphus in October'

claims.claim: It asks whether life is worth living.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [intro]: 'only one really serious philosophical question, and that is suicide'
claims.note: 'Worth living' wording appears verbatim only in iep-existentialism [f. Camus] (not cited); the suicide question clearly entails it.

claims.claim: It does so through Sisyphus forever pushing his rock.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [intro]: 'Sisyphus endlessly pushing his rock up the mountain'

claims.claim: Being and Nothingness is by Jean-Paul Sartre, 1943.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [4.1 Negation and Freedom]: 'Being and Nothingness (1943) remains the defining treatise'

claims.claim: It is the movement's defining treatise.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [4.1]: 'the defining treatise of the existentialist "movement"'
claims.note: SEP adds 'along with works from de Beauvoir'; acceptable compression.

claims.claim: It covers radical freedom.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [4.1]: 'this quite radical philosophy of freedom'

claims.claim: It covers bad faith.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [4.2]: 'the chapter on bad faith in Being and Nothingness'

claims.claim: It covers the look.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [4.3]: 'his writings on the Look of the Other'

claims.claim: Existentialism Is a Humanism is by Jean-Paul Sartre.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [intro]: 'his public lecture, Existentialism is a Humanism'

claims.claim: Its year is 1945; it was a 1945 Paris lecture.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [intro]: 'Many thousands of Parisians packed into ... towards the end of 1945'
claims.note: Learner flag: the same SEP entry ([1. Life and Works]) dates the written text 'completing Existentialism is a Humanism (1946)'. The note says 'lecture', which explains 1945, so not a fail.

claims.claim: The lecture was packed.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [intro]: 'Many thousands of Parisians packed into his public lecture'

claims.claim: It is an accessible version of Being and Nothingness.
claims.evidence: sep-sartre.txt [intro]: 'offered an accessible version of his difficult treatise, Being and Nothingness'

claims.claim: The Second Sex is by Simone de Beauvoir, 1949.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [e. Beauvoir]: 'In 1949 Le Deuxième Sexe is published in France'

claims.claim: It shows how women are made man's 'Other'.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [e. Beauvoir]: 'tradition has always thought of woman as the other of man'

claims.claim: It is a founding text of second-wave feminism.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [e. Beauvoir]: 'later a founding text of Second Wave Feminism'

claims.claim: In Germany, Adorno's The Jargon of Authenticity called existentialism, and Heidegger above all, obscure, abstract and even mystical.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: '(and especially Heidegger) ... obscure, abstract or even mystical ... especially by Adorno'

claims.claim: Many analytic philosophers agreed.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: 'The criticism was echoed by many in the analytic tradition'

claims.claim: After Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s, Sartre decided his early radical freedom was too abstract.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [4.2 Mediated Freedom]: 'in the wake of Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s ... far too abstract'

claims.claim: It ignored the social conditions that limit real choices.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [4.2]: 'failed to engage the social, historical, and material conditions that ... limit'

claims.claim: Merleau-Ponty objected that no one is free in isolation from others and history.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [e. Beauvoir]: 'One cannot assume freedom in isolation from the freedom of others ... historical context'

claims.claim: Later, French structuralists faulted Sartre for neglecting language and impersonal structures of meaning.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: 'insufficient attention to the nature of language and to impersonal structures of meaning'

claims.claim: Existentialists were accused of neglecting social and political structures, with dangerous results.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: 'insufficient attention to social and political structures or values, with dangerous results'

claims.claim: Heidegger remains notorious for his involvement with National Socialism.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [c. Heidegger]: 'remains notorious for his involvement with National Socialism in the 1930s'

claims.claim: Nietzsche's ideal of the self-creating individual is openly elitist and anti-democratic.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [5.3]: 'his account of authenticity is unapologetically elitist and anti-democratic'
claims.note: SEP states this descriptively, not as a criticism; placing it under 'criticisms' is a mild framing choice, acceptable.

claims.claim: Nazi ideologues exploited his work, in a way the IEP calls 'utterly misdirected'.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Nietzsche]: 'exploitation of his teaching by the Nazi ideologues ... although utterly misdirected'
claims.note: IEP adds it 'arguably had its source in Nietzsche's own "aristocratic radicalism"'; omission is not misleading.

claims.claim: Camus accused Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger of escaping into 'forced hope'.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [3.3]: against 'Shestov, Kierkegaard, Jaspers, and Heidegger ... That forced hope is religious in all of them'

claims.claim: Some argue the label does more harm than good, lumping very different ideas together.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'conflate together significantly different ideas – does more harm than good'

claims.claim: Existentialism reached into films by Bergman and Godard.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'films by Ingmar Bergman ... Jean-Luc Godard'

claims.claim: It reached the theatre of the absurd and Beckett.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [a. The Arts and Psychology]: 'the theatre of the absurd and most obviously Beckett were influenced'

claims.claim: It reached painting from Munch to Hopper.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'paintings of Edvard Munch ... and Edward Hopper'

claims.claim: Its stress on freedom fed the politics of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'emphasis on freedom ... informed the ... politics of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X'

claims.claim: It fed the writing of Richard Wright and Ralph Ellison.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'writings of Black intellectuals such as Ralph Ellison, Richard Wright'

claims.claim: Beauvoir laid foundations for second-wave feminism.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.4]: 'laying the conceptual foundations for second wave feminism'

claims.claim: Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks drew on Beauvoir, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.4]: 'Together with Sartre and Merleau-Ponty, her ideas would inform Franz Fanon's Black Skin'

claims.claim: It inspired existential psychotherapy, from Viktor Frankl to Rollo May and Irvin Yalom.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'existential approaches to psychotherapy ... Rollo May, Viktor Frankl, and Irvin Yalom'

claims.claim: The IEP judges the movement as a whole has had relatively little direct influence in academic philosophy.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: 'existentialism has had relatively little direct influence within philosophy'

claims.claim: Nietzsche and Heidegger remain very much alive there.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: 'Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular are very much "live" topics'

claims.claim: The SEP sees it thriving.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7. Contemporary Relevance]: 'the movement continues to thrive in the academy today'

claims.claim: It shaped Foucault and Derrida.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.1]: Nietzsche and Heidegger 'decisive influences' on Derrida and Foucault

claims.claim: It shaped theories of the self as a life story.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.2]: 'informed key developments in narrative ... philosophy ... grasp our lives in a narrative'

claims.claim: It shaped cognitive science's picture of the embodied mind.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.3]: 'replaced the picture of the disembodied mind with ... embodied self'

claims.claim: It made emotion a serious subject.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [b. Philosophy]: importance placed on emotion, 'legitimising a whole domain of philosophical research'

claims.claim: It made topics like death and illness serious subjects.
claims.evidence: iep [b. Philosophy]: philosophy 'should deal very directly with "real world" topics such as sex, death or crime'; sep [7.6] on health professions
claims.note: Overstated: the sources say existentialism made philosophy treat death directly rather than abstractly, not that it made death a serious subject (death was a central philosophical topic long before). 'Illness' comes from SEP 7.6, which is about influence on clinical and allied health practice, not philosophy taking up illness.

claims.claim: Its courses remain among philosophy's most popular.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [7.7]: 'Existentialist-themed courses are often among the most popular in the philosophy curriculum'

fix_hint: Replace 'It made emotion, and topics like death and illness, serious subjects' with something like 'It gave emotion a place in serious research, and insisted philosophy deal directly with real-life topics like death; its first-person view of illness has also shaped medicine and nursing.'

claims.claim: Existentialism is a loose movement that begins from concrete human existence.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'not ... a coherent system'; 'begins in medias res, amidst our own situated, first-person experience'

claims.claim: It is rooted in Kierkegaard and Nietzsche.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'groundwork ... laid much earlier ... by pioneers like Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche'

claims.claim: It was made famous by Sartre and Beauvoir in mid-20th-century France.
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism.txt [intro]: 'most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably ... Sartre and ... Beauvoir'

claims.claim: The six themes named are the pilot's six themes.
claims.evidence: pilot themes[]: existence before essence; freedom and anxiety; authenticity...; meaning without guarantees; my freedom needs yours; faith and the leap
claims.note: Prompt says 'authenticity and bad faith' where the theme is titled 'Authenticity versus the crowd'; the theme body covers bad faith, so coverage holds. Consider matching the title.

claims.claim: Camus rejected the existentialist label.
claims.evidence: sep-camus.txt [1. The Paradoxes...]: 'Camus denied being an existentialist'

claims.claim: Heidegger rejected the existentialist label.
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism.txt [c. Heidegger]: 'given Heidegger's own repudiation of existentialism'
claims.note: Heidegger is not in the pilot's thinkers list but is covered in origins, key works and criticisms, so naming him stays within the pilot.
